title: Yara and the Cellar
premise: Juniper Pemberton arrives in the village of Hollowmere to appraise Yarrow House, a property whose measurements refuse to stay written down — rooms grow between surveys, and the cellar stairs count differently each time he descends. He befriends Yara, the house's last reluctant heir, who knows the cellar holds the melted bell of 1911 and that its song still wants a voice. When the phantom bell rings and pulls Juniper into its congregation of the documented dead, he must learn the song's final verse from Yara's grandmother's suppressed hymnal without ever singing along, because a verse learned aloud is a verse owed. In the climax Juniper transcribes the verse instead of singing it, feeding the bell paper instead of breath, and the house releases him — but Yara, who chose loyalty to her family's secret over truth, must decide whether to let him leave or follow the song herself; she stays, and the house finally lets its ledger close.
about_author: Oscar Lockridge is the pen name of a former land surveyor who spent eleven years measuring houses across the English moors before turning to horror. He writes in the margins of old property deeds and claims none of his stories are invented, only transcribed.

chapters.title: The Measurements Refuse
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Arriving at Yarrow House to appraise it for sale, he meets Yara, the heir who never wanted it, and begins documenting anomalies: stair counts that change, doorways absent from the 1911 plans. Emotional beat: professional detachment curdling into unease as his careful records become the only thing anchoring the house to reality.

chapters.title: What the Bell Was Before
chapters.summary: Alternating Juniper and Yara POVs. Yara reveals the bell was melted in 1911 after three singers vanished mid-hymn, and shows him her grandmother's hymnal with the last verse torn out. At dusk the bell rings anyway. Emotional beat: intimacy and dread braided together as belonging to someone becomes indistinguishable from belonging to the house.

chapters.title: Congregation of the Documented
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Pulled into the cellar during the ringing, he finds the vanished singers preserved as entries in a living ledger, each one a perfectly documented life with no ending. The bell offers him a place among them if he sings. Emotional beat: terror of erasure versus the seductive comfort of being fully recorded, known, kept.

chapters.title: The Verse Written, Not Sung
chapters.summary: Juniper and Yara POVs converge. With time collapsing, Yara chooses truth over family loyalty and recites the torn verse silently while Juniper transcribes it, offering the bell ink instead of voice. The ledger closes; the house goes quiet. Yara stays by choice; Juniper leaves with a survey that finally measures true. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into release.
